---- GND\nESP32 GPIO ---- resistor ---- 2N3904 base\n```\n\nIf yes, then your **2N3904 is acting as an inverter/open-collector gate driver**.\n\n## What this does\n\nWhen ESP32 output is **HIGH**:\n\n```text id=\"7wcofh\"\n2N3904 turns ON\nIRF540N gate is pulled LOW\nMOSFET turns OFF\nLED turns OFF\n```\n\nWhen ESP32 output is **LOW**:\n\n```text id=\"txo5hw\"\n2N3904 turns OFF\n10 kΩ pulls IRF540N gate up to 12 V\nMOSFET turns ON strongly\nLED turns ON\n```\n\nSo your signal is **inverted**:\n\n```text id=\"ouwctx\"\nESP32 HIGH = LED OFF\nESP32 LOW  = LED ON\n```\n\nThat also explains why idle-state matters a lot in your code.\n\n## Is 12 V on the IRF540N gate okay?\n\nUsually yes, **if the MOSFET source is connected to ground**.\n\nFor IRF540N:\n\n```text id=\"zkio8a\"\nVGS = gate voltage - source voltage\nVGS ≈ 12 V - 0 V = 12 V\n```\n\nThat is okay because many MOSFETs allow up to around ±20 V gate-source. But do **not** exceed that.\n\n## Main issue: 10 kΩ is slow for MOSFET gate drive\n\nYour 10 kΩ pull-up is safe, but it charges the IRF540N gate slowly.\n\nAt 10 kHz:\n\n```text id=\"sxow94\"\nhalf-bit = 50 µs\n```\n\nThe IRF540N has a fairly large gate capacitance. With a 10 kΩ pull-up, the gate may not rise fast enough, so the LED transition becomes rounded instead of sharp.\n\nThat can cause:\n\n```text id=\"4jwaqt\"\nCRC fail at higher frequency\nreduced brightness\nmore visible flicker\nMOSFET heating\nslower optical edges\n```\n\n## Better resistor value\n\nTry lowering the gate pull-up resistor:\n\n```text id=\"hhyoei\"\n10 kΩ  → current setup, safer but slower\n4.7 kΩ → better\n2.2 kΩ → faster\n1 kΩ   → fastest among these, but wastes more current\n```\n\nMy recommendation:\n\n```text id=\"6n11fb\"\nTry 2.2 kΩ first\n```\n\nWith 2.2 kΩ:\n\n```text id=\"00t4vj\"\nPull-up current when 2N3904 is ON ≈ 12 V / 2.2 kΩ ≈ 5.45 mA\n```\n\nThat is fine for a 2N3904.\n\nWith 1 kΩ:\n\n```text id=\"xnz6dr\"\nPull-up current ≈ 12 mA\nPower in resistor ≈ 0.144 W\n```\n\nStill possible with a 1/4 W resistor, but 2.2 kΩ is a better first choice.\n\n## Make sure you have a base resistor\n\nDo not connect ESP32 directly to the 2N3904 circuit should look like this\n\n```text id=\"4sxcfs\"\nESP32 GPIO\n   |\n  2.2 kΩ\n   |\n2N3904 base\n\n2N3904 emitter → GND\n\n2N3904 collector ---- IRF540N gate\n        |\n       2.2 kΩ\n        |\n       +12 V\n\n\n+12 V → LED/bulb → IRF540N drain\nIRF540N source → GND\n```\n\n## Important code note\n\nBecause this driver is inverted:\n\n```text id=\"6y45o9\"\nESP32 LOW  = LED ON\nESP32 HIGH = LED OFF\n```\n\nSo if your code assumes active-HIGH LED, it is backwards.\n\nYou either need to invert the TX output in code, or define:\n\n```cpp id=\"oqppgc\"\n#define LED_ON  LOW\n#define LED_OFF HIGH\n```\n\nFor your setup, idle LED ON means the ESP32 pin should idle **LOW**, not HIGH.\n\n## Best improvement\n\nYour circuit is usable, but for cleaner high-speed switching, the best upgrade TX chain explains a lot:\n\n```text\nESP32 → 2N3904 → IRF540N → 12 V LED/bulb\n```\n\nThis can work, but there are **3 important concerns**.\n\n## 1. IRF540N is not ideal for ESP32 logic\n\nThe **IRF540N is not a logic-level MOSFET**. It usually needs a higher gate voltage, commonly around **10 V gate drive**, to fully turn on with low resistance.\n\nYour ESP32 only outputs:\n\n```text\n3.3 V\n```\n\nSo if the IRF540N gate is only being driven near 3.3 V, it may not fully turn on. That causes:\n\n```text\nless brightness\nmore heating\nlower LED power\nonly around 3 W instead of expected 12 W\n```\n\nBetter MOSFET choices:\n\n```text\nIRL540N\nIRLZ44N\nFQP30N06L\nAO3400 / AO3400A for smaller loads\nlogic-level MOSFET with low RDS(on) at VGS = 2.5 V or 4.5 V\n```\n\nThe **L** in IRL usually means logic-level.\n\n## 2. The 2N3904 stage may be inverting your signal\n\nDepending on your circuit, the 2N3904 may invert the ESP32 signal.\n\nCommon NPN gate-pull-down circuit:\n\n```text\nESP32 HIGH → 2N3904 ON → MOSFET gate pulled LOW → LED OFF\nESP32 LOW  → 2N3904 OFF → MOSFET gate pulled HIGH → LED ON\n```\n\nSo your data may be inverted.\n\nThat is not automatically bad, because the RX can still decode if the code expects it, but it matters for:\n\n```text\nidle state\ndefault LED ON/OFF\nManchester polarity\nvisible flicker\n```\n\nIf your idle state is wrong, the bulb may blink or stay dim between frames.\n\n## 3. The 2N3904 + gate resistor may switch the MOSFET too slowly\n\nAt 10 kHz, your half-bit is:\n\n```text\n50 µs\n```\n\nThe MOSFET gate must charge and discharge cleanly within that time. If the IRF540N gate is charged through a large resistor, or discharged weakly through the 2N3904, the LED edges become slow.\n\nSlow edges cause:\n\n```text\nreceiver timing errors\nCRC fail at higher frequency\nvisible brightness fluctuation\nlower optical modulation quality\n```\n\n## Better TX driver design\n\nFor your current prototype, I recommend this:\n\n```text\nESP32 GPIO → 100 Ω gate resistor → logic-level N-MOSFET gate\nMOSFET source → GND\nMOSFET drain → LED negative\nLED positive → +12 V\n10 kΩ gate pulldown → GND\n```\n\nLike this:\n\n```text\n+12 V  →  LED/bulb  →  MOSFET drain\n                         MOSFET source → GND\n\nESP32 GPIO ──100Ω── MOSFET gate\n                    |\n                   10kΩ\n                    |\n                   GND\n```\n\nUse a **logic-level MOSFET**, not IRF540N.\n\n## If you want stronger/faster switching\n\nUse a MOSFET gate driver IC:\n\n```text\nESP32 → TC4420 / TC4427 / MIC4427 / IR4427 → MOSFET → LED\n```\n\nThis gives fast gate charging/discharging and more stable 10 kHz+ modulation.\n\n## For flicker and eye strain\n\nYour current method likely does this:\n\n```text\ndata 1 = LED fully ON\ndata 0 = LED fully OFF\n```\n\nThat causes visible brightness changes, especially with frame gaps.\n\nBetter thesis design:\n\n```text\nMain bulb brightness = steady ON\nData modulation = small high-speed ripple\n```\n\nOr easiest practical version:\n\n```text\nUse the 12 W bulb for room lighting\nUse a separate high-speed LED/IR LED for data\n```\n\nThat gives better comfort and a cleaner receiver signal.\n\n## My recommendation for your exact chain\n\nFor now:\n\n```text\nReplace IRF540N with IRL540N or IRLZ44N\nTry removing the 2N3904 stage first\nDrive the logic-level MOSFET gate directly from ESP32 through 100 Ω\nAdd 10 kΩ gate pulldown to GND\nKeep idle LED ON in code\n```\n\nYour current chain can transmit, but it is not ideal for brightness or high-speed stability. **ACK is feasible**, but for your ceiling-bulb setup, it becomes mechanically and optically harder.\n\nYour current main link is:\n\n```text\nCeiling TX bulb/LED  ↓ light data ↓  RX phototransistor\n```\n\nFor ACK/NACK, you would need a reverse optical link:\n\n```text\nRX side LED/IR LED  ↑ ACK/NACK light ↑  photodiode/phototransistor near ceiling TX\n```\n\nThat means the ceiling transmitter must also have a **receiver sensor** facing downward, and the mobile/desk receiver must also have a **small LED/IR LED transmitter** facing upward.\n\n## Is optical ACK/NACK feasible?\n\nYes, but with issues:\n\n```text\nPros:\n- Pure LiFi/optical, thesis-friendly\n- Allows retransmission of failed chunks\n- More complete communication system\n\nCons:\n- More hardware\n- RX side must aim its ACK LED upward\n- Ceiling TX needs a second receiver circuit\n- Reverse path changes when you change height/distance\n- ACK may fail even if forward data works\n```\n\nSince your experiment needs to test different height distances, optical ACK can make testing more complicated because you would be testing **two links at the same time**:\n\n```text\nForward link: ceiling LED → RX phototransistor\nReverse link: RX ACK LED → ceiling receiver\n```\n\nIf transfer fails, you may not know immediately whether the failure came from the forward data link or the reverse ACK link.\n\n## Better alternative for your setup\n\nFor your ceiling prototype, I recommend a **one-way chunked carousel/repetition protocol** instead of ACK.\n\nThis keeps the system like this:\n\n```text\nCeiling TX bulb/LED  ↓ light data only ↓  RX phototransistor\n```\n\nNo reverse channel needed.\n\n## How one-way carousel transfer works\n\nInstead of sending the file once:\n\n```text\nChunk 0\nChunk 1\nChunk 2\nChunk 3\nEND\n```\n\nThe TX repeatedly sends all chunks in a loop:\n\n```text\nChunk 0\nChunk 1\nChunk 2\nChunk 3\nChunk 0\nChunk 1\nChunk 2\nChunk 3\nChunk 0\nChunk 1\nChunk 2\nChunk 3\n...\n```\n\nThe RX checks CRC for every chunk. If a chunk is valid, it stores it. If a chunk is corrupted, it ignores it and waits for the next round.\n\nExample:\n\n```text\nRound 1:\nChunk 0 OK\nChunk 1 FAIL\nChunk 2 OK\nChunk 3 FAIL\n\nRound 2:\nChunk 1 OK\nChunk 3 OK\n\nFile complete.\n```\n\nThis solves the main problem without ACK.\n\n## Why this is better for your thesis\n\nThis is very suitable for your ceiling-distance testing because the transmitter does not need to know whether the receiver got the data. The receiver simply collects valid chunks until the file is complete.\n\nIt is also closer to real ceiling-light broadcasting:\n\n```text\nOne ceiling light can broadcast data.\nAny receiver under the light can collect the data.\nNo pairing needed.\nNo Wi-Fi.\nNo Bluetooth.\nNo reverse optical link required.\n```\n\nThat is actually a strong LiFi concept.\n\n## Recommended protocol\n\nUse this frame format:\n\n```text\nPREAMBLE\nFRAME_TYPE\nFILE_ID\nTOTAL_SIZE\nTOTAL_CHUNKS\nCHUNK_INDEX\nCHUNK_LENGTH\nCHUNK_CRC\nFILE_CRC\nPAYLOAD\n```\n\nThe RX keeps a checklist:\n\n```text\nChunk 0: received\nChunk 1: missing\nChunk 2: received\nChunk 3: missing\n```\n\nWhen all chunks are received:\n\n```text\nRebuild file\nCheck full-file CRC\nSave file\nShow RX_FILE_CRC_OK\n```\n\n## Best option comparison\n\n| Method | Feasible for ceiling setup? | Thesis-friendly? | Recommendation |\n|---|---:|---:|---|\n| Wi-Fi ACK | Easy | No | Avoid |\n| Bluetooth ACK | Easy | No | Avoid |\n| Optical ACK/NACK | Feasible but harder | Yes | Good advanced feature |\n| Repeated chunks | Very feasible | Yes | Best next step |\n| Forward error correction | Feasible but more complex | Yes | Future upgrade |\n| SD card standalone transfer | Very feasible | Yes | Good final prototype |\n\n## My recommendation\n\nFor your actual prototype, use:\n\n```text\nMain method:\nOne-way chunked carousel transfer with CRC\n\nOptional advanced feature:\nOptical ACK/NACK only as a future improvement\n```\n\nThis will work better with your ceiling bulb, height-distance testing, and thesis requirements.\n\nFor your next code upgrade, the best direction is:\n\n```text\nChunked transfer without ACK\nRepeated carousel mode\nRX collects only valid chunks\nFull-file CRC check at the end\n```\n\nThat will let you send text, images, audio, and eventually video more reliably without needing Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, or a reverse optical self.add_rx_log(f\"RX read error: {e}\")\n                break\n            if not data:\n                continue\n            self.rx_buffer.extend(data)\n            self.process_rx_buffer()\n\n    def process_rx_buffer(self):\n        while self.rx_buffer:\n            if self.expecting_raw is not None:\n                tid, seq, length = self.expecting_raw\n                if len(self.rx_buffer) < length:\n                    return\n                raw = bytes(self.rx_buffer[:length])\n                del self.rx_buffer[:length]\n                # RX prints a newline after exact binary data. Remove it as delimiter.\n                if self.rx_buffer.startswith(b\"\\r\\n\"):\n                    del self.rx_buffer[:2]\n                elif self.rx_buffer.startswith(b\"\\n\"):\n                    del self.rx_buffer[:1]\n                with self.chunk_condition:\n                    self.chunk_data[(tid, seq)] = raw\n                    self.chunk_condition.notify_all()\n                self.add_rx_log(f\"RX chunk data tid={tid} seq={seq} bytes={length}\")\n                self.expecting_raw = None\n                continue\n\n            newline = self.rx_buffer.find(b\"\\n\")\n            if newline < 0:\n                return\n            line_bytes = bytes(self.rx_buffer[:newline + 1])\n            del self.rx_buffer[:newline + 1]\n            line = line_bytes.decode(\"utf-8\", errors=\"replace\").strip(\"\\r\\n\")\n            if not line:\n                continue\n            self.handle_rx_line(line)\n\n    def handle_rx_line(self, line: str):\n        if line.startswith(\"RX_CHUNK_DATA:\"):\n            try:\n                _, tid, seq, length = line.split(\":\", 3)\n                self.expecting_raw = (int(tid), int(seq), int(length))\n            except Exception:\n                self.add_rx_log(f\"Malformed chunk data line: {line}\")\n            return\n\n        if line.startswith(\"RX_CHUNK_OK:\"):\n            self.add_rx_log(line)\n            try:\n                parts = line.split(\":\")\n                tid = int(parts[1])\n                seq = int(parts[2])\n                with self.chunk_condition:\n                    self.chunk_ack[(tid, seq)] = \"ok\"\n                    self.chunk_condition.notify_all()\n            except Exception:\n                pass\n            return\n\n        if line.startswith(\"RX_CHUNK_FAIL:\"):\n            self.add_rx_log(line)\n            try:\n                parts = line.split(\":\")\n                tid = int(parts[1])\n                seq = int(parts[2])\n                with self.chunk_condition:\n                    self.chunk_ack[(tid, seq)] = \"fail\"\n                    self.chunk_condition.notify_all()\n            except Exception:\n                pass\n            return\n\n        # Other RX messages: frequency, debug, legacy logs, etc.\n        self.add_rx_log(line)\n\n    # ---------------- Transfer logic ----------------\n    def get_chunk_size(self) -> int:\n        try:\n            size = int(self.chunk_size_var.get())\n        except ValueError:\n            size = 512\n        return max(128, try:\n            return max(1, min(50000, int(self.freq_var.get().strip())))\n        except Exception:\n            return 10000\n\n    def start_transfer(self, data: bytes, kind: int, name: str):\n        self.transfer_running = True\n        self.progress[\"value\"] = 0\n        self.progress_label.config(text=\"0% | ETA --\")\n        t = threading.Thread(target=self.transfer_worker, self.get_chunk_size()\n        total_size = len(data)\n        total_chunks = (total_size + chunk_size - 1) // chunk_size\n        max_retries = self.get_retries()\n        start = time.time()\n        retries_used = 0\n\n        kind_name = KIND_NAMES.get(kind, \"file\")\n        self.set_status(f\"Sending {kind_name} in {total_chunks} chunks...\", \"blue\")\n        self.add_tx_log(f\"Chunked      if kind != KIND_TEXT:\n            self.receive_folder = self.folder_entry.get().strip() or self.receive_folder\n            os.makedirs(self.receive_folder, exist_ok=True)\n return\n\n        ok = False\n        try:\n            for seq in range(total_chunks):\n                offset = seq * chunk_size\n                chunk = data[offset: offset + chunk_size]\n\n                sent_ok = False\n                for attempt in range(max_retries + 1):\n                    if attempt > 0:\n                        retries_used += 1\n                        self.add_tx_log(f\"Retry chunk {seq + 1}/{total_chunks}, attempt {attempt}/{max_retries}\")\n\n                    self.clear_chunk_result(transfer_id, seq)\n total_chunks: int, total_size: int, chunk: bytes):\n        payload = struct.pack(\">HBHHIH\", tid, kind, seq, total_chunks, total_size, len(chunk)) + chunk\n        if len(payload) > 0xFFFF:\n            raise ValueError(\"Chunk payload too large\")\n        crc = crc16_ccitt(payload)\n        header = bytes([\n            START_BYTE,\n            TYPE_CHUNK_CRC,\n            (len(payload) >> 8) & 0xFF,\n            len(payload) & 0xFF,\n            (crc >> 8) & 0xFF,\n            crc & 0xFF,\n        ])\n        self.tx_serial.write(header + payload)\n        self.tx_serial.flush()\n        self.add_tx_log(f\"Sent chunk {seq + 1}/{total_chunks} ({len(chunk)} bytes), crc=0x{crc:04X}\")\n\n    def estimate_chunk_timeout(self, payload_len: int) -> float:\n        freq = According to Albert Einstein, mass and energy are interchangeable under certain circumstances. When atoms split, the process is called nuclear fission. Examples #1\r\n03:33:16 RX: RX: Why do Atoms Explode when they are Split?\r\n03:33:16 RX: RX: \r\n03:33:16 RX: RX: Atoms of radioactive elements can split. According to Albert Einstein, mass and energy are interchangeable under certain circumstances. When atoms split, the process is called nuclear fission. In this case, a small amount of mass is converted into energy. Thus the energy released cannot do much damage. However, several subatomic particles called neutrons are also emitted during this process. Each neutron will hit a radioactive element releasing more neutrons in the process. This causes a chain reaction and creates a large amount of energy. This energy is converted into heat which expands uncontrollably causing an explosion. Hence, atoms do not literally explode. They generate energy that can cause explosions.\r\n03:33:16 RX: RX: \r\n03:33:16 RX: RX: Short Paragraph Examples #2\r\n03:33:16 RX: RX: WOMAN’S DAY\r\n03:33:16 RX: RX: \r\n03:33:16 RX: RX: Since March 8, 1990, Women’s Day has been observed by SAARC (South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation) comprising seven countries namely India, Pakistan, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Maldives. The day is celebrated to highlight the problems of the girl child in these countries. It is very sad that girl children are subjected to extreme neglect and disrespect, especially in underdeveloped countries. The birth of a girl child is seen by parents as a cause of pity. They are deprived of proper nutrition, education, economic opportunities and social status or respect. That is why no received text appears.\n\n## Main cause\n\nThere are two issues happening:\n\n### 1. ESP32 resets when the GUI opens the COM port\n\nThis is normal for many ESP32 boards. When Python opens the serial port, the ESP32 auto-resets. Your GUI sends `FREQ=1000` too early, while the ESP32 is still booting. Sometimes the command is missed.\n\n### 2. RX code blocks while waiting for optical data\n\nYour RX code waits inside the Manchester receiver loop. Atoms of radioactive elements can split. According to Albert Einstein, mass and energy are interchangeable under certain circumstances. When atoms split, the process is called nuclear fission. In this case, a small amount of mass is converted into energy. Thus the energy released cannot do much damage. However, several subatomic particles called neutrons are also emitted during this process. Each neutron will hit a radioactive element releasing more neutrons in the process. This causes a chain reaction and creates a large amount of energy. This energy is converted into heat which expands uncontrollably causing an explosion. Hence, atoms do not literally explode. 1500hz\n\ni sent this text 3 times\n\nShort Paragraph Examples #1\r\nWhy do Atoms Explode when they are Split?\r\n\r\nAtoms of radioactive elements can split. According to Albert Einstein, mass and energy are interchangeable under certain circumstances. When atoms split, the process is called nuclear fission. In this case, a small amount of mass is converted into energy. Thus the energy released cannot do much damage. However, several subatomic particles called neutrons are also emitted during this process. Each neutron will hit a radioactive element releasing more neutrons in the process. This causes a chain reaction and creates a large amount of energy. This energy is converted into heat which expands uncontrollably causing an explosion. Hence, atoms do not literally explode. They generate energy that can cause explosions.\r\n\r\nShort Paragraph Examples #2\r\nWOMAN’S DAY\r\n\r\nSince March 8, 1990, Women’s Day has been observed by SAARC (South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation) comprising seven countries namely India, Pakistan, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Maldives. new error is **not mainly CRC anymore**. This time the problem is **TX serial overflow / no flow control**.\n\nYour GUI sends text as **128-byte chunks**, writes the header + chunk to the TX ESP32, then waits only **0.01 second** before sending the next chunk. fileciteturn6file0L340-L367 Your log says the 588-byte text became **5 chunks**, so the GUI is pushing those chunks almost immediately. fileciteturn6file0L369-L370\n\nBut at **500 Hz Manchester**, one 128-byte chunk takes about:\n\n```text\n1 byte ≈ 10 Manchester bit periods\n1 byte at 500 Hz ≈ 10 / 500 = 0.02 s\n128 bytes ≈ 2.56 s\nplus header + preamble ≈ around 3 seconds per chunk\n```\n\nSo the GUI sends the next chunks after **10 ms**, while the TX ESP32 still needs around **3 seconds** to finish transmitting the first chunk optically.\n\nThat is why your received text jumps like this:\n\n```text\n... In this case, a smalons in the process ...\n```\n\nIt received the earlier part, then skipped a large middle section. This means some chunks were lost while the TX ESP32 was still busy transmitting the previous data.\n\n## Main cause\n\nYour current TX code reads from USB serial and transmits optically at the same time, byte-by-byte:\n\n```cpp\nread 1 byte from Serial\nsend that byte using Manchester\nread next byte\nsend next byte\n```\n\nThat is too slow. The PC keeps sending data much faster than the ESP32 can transmit through light, so the ESP32 serial buffer overflows.\n\n## Fix I prepared\n\nUse these updated files:\n\n[Download fixed GUI with TX wait/ACK](sandbox:/mnt/data/file_transfer_gui_ack_fixed.py)\n\n[Download fixed TX ESP32 buffered code](sandbox:/mnt/data/tx_esp32_buffered_ack.ino)\n\n[Download fixed RX ESP32 CRC-order code](sandbox:/mnt/data/rx_file_transfer_crc_fixed.ino)\n\n## What changed\n\nThe fixed **TX ESP32** now does this:\n\n```text\n1. Receive the full payload from the GUI quickly\n2. Store it in ESP32 RAM\n3. Then transmit it optically using Manchester\n4. Print “TX: text chunk sent”\n```\n\nThe fixed **GUI** now waits for that TX done message before sending the next text chunk.\n\nSo instead of this bad flow:\n\n```text\nGUI sends chunk 1\nwait 0.01s\nGUI sends chunk 2\nwait 0.01s\nGUI sends chunk 3\nTX ESP32 overflows\n```\n\nIt becomes:\n\n```text\nGUI sends chunk 1\nTX ESP32 transmits chunk 1 optically\nTX says done\nGUI sends chunk 2\nTX ESP32 transmits chunk 2 optically\nTX says done\n...\n```\n\n## Also: your RX log showing `RX: RX:`\n\nThat part is not a transmission bug. Your ESP32 receiver prints:\n\n```text\nRX: message\n```\n\nThen your GUI also prefixes the log with:\n\n```text\nRX:\n```\n\nSo it appears as:\n\n```text\nRX: RX: message\n```\n\nYou can ignore that for now.\n\n## Best method for text, image, and future audio\n\nFor your current LiFi project, the best method is:\n\n```text\nManchester encoding + framed packets + CRC + ACK per chunk\n```\n\nFor text: small chunks are okay.  \nFor image/file: use binary packets with CRC and ACK.  \nFor future audio: do not start with live audio yet. First make file transfer reliable. Then send small compressed audio files like `.wav` or `.mp3`. Real-time audio will need much higher frequency than 500 Hz.",{},{"_615":8548,"_622":8618,"_34":8619,"_626":8620,"_628":629,"_630":14,"_631":632,"_633":8621,"_635":636},"cce5e130-5fec-4ec7-bf5c-f9a5c25c88d8",[8531],{"_700":701,"_633":8626},1778177083.178547,{"_695":719,"_626":8625},{"_710":711,"_712":8622,"_714":8623,"_716":8624,"_653":8561,"_655":656,"_657":8562,"_659":47,"_46":47,"_660":661,"_662":14,"_663":8616,"_664":8563,"_666":26,"_667":8564,"_669":10},150,1778176932.5387821,1778177083.170116,"Thought for 2m 30s",{},{"_615":8616,"_622":8630,"_34":8631,"_626":8632,"_628":629,"_630":14,"_631":632,"_633":8633,"_635":636},"3037d4a4-7642-4710-aed7-9151672d5d6a",[8548],{"_700":701,"_633":8646},1778177080.57907,{"_695":739,"_739":8637,"_741":8636},{"_710":729,"_642":8634,"_644":8635,"_648":47,"_732":26,"_733":26,"_734":632,"_653":8561,"_655":656,"_657":8562,"_659":47,"_46":47,"_660":661,"_663":8636,"_736":78,"_714":8623,"_737":738,"_662":14,"_664":8563,"_666":26,"_667":8564,"_669":10},[],[],"893071cb-6b00-4419-a533-16c628a47ac3",[8638],{"_743":8639,"_626":8640,"_746":8641,"_748":26},"Finalizing citation details for code","I need to make the final version concise, but also include relevant details and citations when necessary. found the cause.\n\nYour **GUI sends this order** for text:\n\n```text\nSTART, TYPE, SIZE_MSB, SIZE_LSB, CRC_MSB, CRC_LSB, PAYLOAD\n```\n\nFor `sad`, your GUI actually sends `sad\\n`, so payload length is **4 bytes**, not 3. The GUI builds the text frame with CRC first, then writes the actual text chunk after the header. fileciteturn3file0\n\nBut your **RX code expects this order**:\n\n```text\nSTART, TYPE, SIZE_MSB, SIZE_LSB, PAYLOAD, CRC_MSB, CRC_LSB\n```\n\nSo for `sad\\n`, this happens:\n\n```text\nCorrect sent frame:\n02 02 00 04 97 96 73 61 64 0A\n            ^^^^^ CRC    ^^^^^^^^^ payload \"sad\\n\"\n\nRX wrongly reads:\npayload = 97 96 73 61\nexpected CRC = 64 0A\n```\n\nThat is why your RX log shows:\n\n```text\nRX_TEXT_CRC_FAIL:F866 expected=640A\n```\n\n`640A` is not the real CRC. It is the ASCII bytes:\n\n```text\n0x64 = 'd'\n0x0A = newline\n```\n\nSo the receiver is accidentally treating the last two payload bytes as the CRC.\n\n## Main fix\n\nFix the **RX code**, not the GUI. The GUI and TX are already using the same format: CRC before payload.\n\nI made a corrected RX file here:\n\n[Download fixed RX INO](sandbox:/mnt/data/rx_file_transfer_fixed.ino)\n\nUpload this to your **receiver ESP32**.\n\n## Also important for file/image transfer\n\nYour old RX code also has a file-transfer problem: it prints `RX_FILE_START` before the full file is validated, then prints progress messages while the GUI is already expecting raw file bytes. That can make the GUI accidentally save log text as file data.\n\nThe fixed RX file changes that behavior:\n\n```text\nReceive optical data first\nCompute CRC\nIf CRC OK:\n    print RX_FILE_START\n    send raw file bytes to GUI\n    print RX_FILE_CRC_OK\n```\n\nThat is safer for images and binary files.\n\n## Best transmission method for your project\n\nFor your current LiFi setup, the best method is:\n\n```text\nManchester encoding + binary packets + CRC + small chunks\n```\n\nUse one frame format for everything:\n\n```text\nPREAMBLE\nSTART\nTYPE\nLENGTH\nCRC\nPAYLOAD\n```\n\nRecommended types:\n\n```text\n0x01 = file/image/audio bytes\n0x02 = text\n0x03 = command/control\n```\n\nFor now, test in this order:\n\n1. Send short text like `sad`\n2. Send longer text\n3. Send a small `.txt` file\n4. Send a very small `.jpg` or `.png`\n5. Then increase frequency slowly\n\nAt **500 Hz**, this is still very slow. Because each byte needs Manchester timing plus start/stop overhead, you may only get around tens of bytes per second. Text is okay, small images are possible but slow, and audio will need a much faster optical link.\n\nFor future audio, do not start with MP3/MP4 yet. First make your binary file transfer reliable, then try small compressed audio files.
